title: AI can create an interface. But who decides if it's good?
description: If AI creates an interface in seconds, who decides if it's good? Why critical judgment and context become the core of UI work.

related.title: Clint Scale
related.body: In practice: an explorable design system, with tokens, components, contrast and governance.

blocks.text: The speed of creating interfaces has changed a lot.
Today we can describe an idea, generate a screen, create variations, turn a layout into code and test different possibilities in a few minutes.
That's a big shift for anyone working in Product Design.

data.lead: But there's a question I think is even more important:
data.q: If AI can create an interface quickly, who decides whether that interface is actually good?
data.after: For me, that question is starting to matter more than the ability to generate screens itself.

blocks.text: Creating got cheaper
For a long time, a big part of UI work was turning an idea into an interface.
You had to open Figma, create frames, organize components, define spacing, choose typography, create states and prepare a prototype.
Today, many of these tasks can be sped up by AI.

items: We can test an idea earlier
We can build more complete prototypes

blocks.text: We can get faster to something we can put in front of a person.
The problem starts when we confuse speed of production with quality of the solution.
An interface can be created in seconds and still be a bad solution.
The problem with the interface that looks right
AI is very good at recognizing patterns.

blocks.caption: The designer's role shifts from producing everything to evaluating, selecting and directing.

data.intro: That means it can produce interfaces that look familiar.
data.ruleNote: But an interface can follow all these rules and still not solve the right problem.
data.pull: A visually good interface isn't necessarily a good experience.
data.l1: It can be beautiful, consistent and technically well built.
questions: But does the user understand it?
Do they trust what they're seeing?

blocks.text: This is where critical judgment comes in
With AI producing more options, the designer's work starts to change.
Instead of spending so much time creating each alternative by hand, we can spend more time comparing alternatives.
And comparing requires criteria.
Why is this solution better?
For which user?
In what context?
What problem does it solve?
What happens when it goes wrong?
What's the impact on the business?
What evidence do we have to defend this choice?
These questions are part of design work.
And they don't disappear because a tool can generate the interface.
Critique is a design skill too

data.lead: There's a difference between looking at an interface and saying:
data.deep: “This solution reduces cognitive load at this step, but it creates a new question about what happens after submitting.”

blocks.text: The second analysis requires UX knowledge.
Critique isn't just pointing out problems.
It's building criteria to decide what should be kept, changed or thrown out.
A good interface needs context
Imagine you ask an AI to create a checkout screen.
It can do it.
But it doesn't automatically know everything you know about that product.
It may not know:

items: the needs of different user profiles;
the decisions the team has already made.

blocks.text: The better the context, the better the result tends to be.
That changes an important part of the designer's work.
It's not just knowing how to write a prompt.
It's knowing what context needs to go into the process.
The designer starts working more like an editor
Maybe this is one of the most interesting changes.

blocks.caption: Speed of production isn't quality of the solution.

blocks.text: The designer checks whether it really represents the intended experience.
In this scenario, the designer is no longer just the one who produces.
They also become the one who edits, questions, selects and directs.
This changes what it means to be good at UI
I don't think UI will stop being important.
Quite the opposite.
Visual fundamentals are still necessary.
But knowing how to build a screen by hand may no longer be as strong a differentiator as it used to be.
If a tool can create a visually acceptable interface in a few seconds, the differentiator moves to other capabilities:
good judgment, repertoire, context, research and the ability to evaluate.
So how do you use AI without losing critical thinking?

data.lead: I like to think of a simple process:
steps: First, we use AI to explore
We test with people or with data
And we use what we learn to improve
The mistake is stopping at the first step
data.a: An interface created by AI is a hypothesis.

blocks.text: The new differentiator
I believe the designer's value will be less and less about producing a screen quickly.
And more and more about knowing which screen is worth producing.
AI can increase our speed.
But we still have to decide where to put that speed.
Because creating more solutions doesn't mean creating better solutions.
And maybe this is one of the most important skills for the Product Designer in the coming years:
knowing how to look at a solution and explain why it should exist.
